title: BBC’s preschool shows to be made available in CBeebies hub on Netflix
summary:
Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee among 24 shows to be trialled on world’s biggest streaming service

Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee are among a host of the BBC’s preschool…

blocks.text: Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee are among a host of the BBC’s preschool shows to be made available on Netflix, as the broadcaster battles to arrest a generational shift away from its programming.

In an unprecedented six-month trial, a dedicated CBeebies hub will be set up on the world’s biggest streaming service, with a substantial selection of 24 shows to choose from. It will include some of the BBC’s best-known titles and characters.
BBC executives said the deal was a “win-win”, allowing the corporation to reach more families and handing Netflix a windfall of quality children’s programming.

It marks the BBC’s latest deal with an “off-platform” provider, having already announced plans to make content designed for YouTube. The shows will be available on Netflix globally apart from in China, New Zealand and South Africa.

While parents and children still report appreciating the BBC’s children’s content, a huge shift to global streaming and digital platforms means gen alpha – people born between 2010 and 2025 – are simply not as reliant on the broadcaster as previous generations.

Having a clearly branded home on Netflix will help ensure viewers continue to associate the programming with the BBC, which has lost 2.7 million payers of the £180 annual licence fee since the beginning of the decade.
When the streaming giant has previously snapped up international rights to hit BBC shows, such as The Bodyguard and Peaky Blinders, it has branded the content as a “Netflix Original”.
However, the educationally focused BBC content will now sit alongside some Netflix kids’ content, such as CoComelon, which has come in for criticism over its fast-pacing leading to overstimulation.

With linear broadcast television reaching just a third of children aged four to 15 in an average week last year, down from 54% in 2022, traditional broadcasters are seeking deals to increase the reach of their shows as viewing habits move to streaming.

Meanwhile, the BBC’s iPlayer has been falling behind. More than 90% of children aged three to 16 say they like the services offered by YouTube, Netflix and Disney. Only 65% of child users say they like using the iPlayer.

The CBeebies deal also helps Netflix, which is itself under pressure from its rival Disney, which has a younger audience, and YouTube. Children in the UK aged four to 15 watch the most YouTube of any age group at home across all devices, averaging 61 minutes a day.
Children are now heading to YouTube from the moment they turn on the television. Netflix is close behind, though BBC One remains in the top five of first TV destinations.
The new Netflix deal will also strengthen the argument that anyone watching a streaming service should pay the BBC’s licence fee.

That proposal is expected to be announced by the government later this year, amid growing concerns that the BBC’s current licence fee model will soon mean the broadcaster is unsustainable without radically reducing its output and remit.
after newsletter promotion
The CBeebies hub will be trialled on Netflix for six months from the start of December. Some CBeebies shows have previously featured on the streamer, but the trial marks an unprecedented expansion.

Patricia Hidalgo, the director of BBC children and education, who has previously raised concerns about the lack of culturally relevant content reaching young children, said it was an opportunity to increase “the amount of content that is homegrown and telling British stories to British children”.
The BBC is now engaging in more deals with streamers and digital services, as it seeks to increase commercial income and remain relevant as audiences fragment.

Hidalgo said the trial would provide a “taster” to Netflix subscribers and would be assessed after six months to see if it was helping the BBC reach new audiences and whether they understood it was BBC content.

Anne Mensah, the head of content for Netflix in the UK, said CBeebies held a “special and unrivalled place in the hearts of UK families and we are delighted to bring that love to all our Netflix homes in the UK and beyond”.
Last month, Channel 4 struck a deal to make a range of its programmes, as well as its flagship channel, available on Disney+ in the UK and Ireland from next year.

The deal goes signifcantly further than a partnership struck by ITV and Disney+ last year in which the two companies agreed to share a selection of shows, including Mr Bates vs The Post Office and Lucasfilm’s Andor, on their respective streaming services.
